The script bootstraps jq from there when the host has none.

{
  "schema": 5,
  "cc_switch_version": "jya0-5.11.1",
  "max_output_tokens": 65536,
  "platforms": [
    {"target": "linux-x64-musl", "archive_ext": "tar.gz"},
    {"target": "linux-arm64-musl", "archive_ext": "tar.gz"},
    {"target": "darwin-universal", "archive_ext": "tar.gz"},
    {"target": "windows-x64", "archive_ext": "zip"}
  ],
  "cc_switch_artifacts": {
    "linux-x64-musl":  {"file": "cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-linux-x64-musl.tar.gz",  "sha256": "..."},
    "linux-arm64-musl":{"file": "cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-linux-arm64-musl.tar.gz","sha256": "..."},
    "darwin-universal":{"file": "cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-darwin-universal.tar.gz","sha256": "..."},
    "windows-x64":     {"file": "cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-windows-x64.zip",        "sha256": "..."}
  },
  "harnesses": {
    "claude":    {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/claude/v2.json",    "sha256": "..."},
    "codex":     {"version": 3, "path": "providers/adeo/codex/v3.json",     "sha256": "..."},
    "gemini":    {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/gemini/v2.json",    "sha256": "..."},
    "open-code": {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/open-code/v2.json", "sha256": "..."},
    "pi":        {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/pi/v2.json",        "sha256": "..."},
    "hermes":    {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/hermes/v2.json",    "sha256": "..."},
    "open-claw": {"version": 2, "path": "providers/adeo/open-claw/v2.json", "sha256": "..."}
  }
}

Only the artifacts for the supported matrix are listed; the admin sync refuses to publish a manifest referencing a missing object (binary or preset).

The starting matrix is deliberately small: Linux x86-64 musl, Linux ARM64 musl, macOS universal, Windows x64. Musl builds are statically linked, so they run on any libc and we do not need separate glibc/musl rows; macOS universal covers both Intel and Apple Silicon. More targets can be added by appending to platforms + cc_switch_artifacts.

docs.title: cc-switch release artifacts
docs.text:
Source: the ADEO fork's GitHub release (github.com/AITDEV00/cc-switch-cli) for the pinned version (jya0-5.11.1 today). The fork carries the provider add --overwrite upsert the installer's same-id refresh depends on; upstream builds do not have it. Naming follows the release scheme verbatim (fork tags carry no leading v, so neither do the asset names):

/install/cc-switch/jya0-5.11.1/cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-linux-x64-musl.tar.gz
/install/cc-switch/jya0-5.11.1/cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-linux-arm64-musl.tar.gz
/install/cc-switch/jya0-5.11.1/cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-darwin-universal.tar.gz
/install/cc-switch/jya0-5.11.1/cc-switch-cli-jya0-5.11.1-windows-x64.zip

The musl builds are statically linked, so the binary runs on any libc — that is why there is no Python/uv/wheelhouse tier at all.

Integrity chain. The fork release publishes a checksums.txt covering every asset. At ingest time the admin sync downloads each archive and verifies it against the release's checksums.txt; only the verified SHA-256 then goes into our manifest.json. The client never sees upstream's checksums file — it trusts only the manifest, which is written over the authenticated admin channel.

Immutability. A cc-switch/<version>/<file> object, once published with a given sha256, is never overwritten with different bytes; a new build gets a new version path. The manifest is published with a generation/ETag so two concurrent admin syncs cannot silently clobber each other (see admin-sync.md).

docs.title: Harness presets — providers/adeo/<harness>/v<N>.json
docs.text:
Every harness owns a versioned preset slice: the canonical cc-switch settings_config skeleton for that harness — the exact shape cc-switch v5.11.1 itself stores — with sentinels where runtime values go. Identical for every user; no per-user data is ever written to the store. Served at /install/providers/adeo/<harness>/v<N>.json (store copy when present, baked fallback otherwise — sync-mirror.sh generates the staged presets from the gateway's baked set, so the two cannot drift).

The manifest pins each harness to a specific version + sha256, so revising a harness's config shape is an independent publish: bump the version, push a new v<N>.json, and repoint the manifest — without touching the installer script, the cc-switch binary, or any other harness.

The per-harness shapes (all verified against the v5.11.1 binary — see installer-script.md step 4 for the compose). Preset v2 adds per-model context windows (context_length from the key-scoped /api/v1/models) wherever the harness has a real knob, plus the manifest's max_output_tokens default for the two harnesses with an output knob. v3 (codex only) adds the modelCatalog block and drops the dead disable_response_storage TOML key (Codex 0.165.0 prints a per-run "unrecognized setting" warning for it). A preset version bump is a new v<N>.json object + a manifest repoint: the old version stays in the store, so mid-flight installers finish against the version they pinned.

Harness Sentinels in preset Notes claude env with ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_MODEL + the three role-model slots, CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS (__DEFAULT_MODEL_CONTEXT__), CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS (__MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS__) what cc-switch's own field-mode add stores, plus the two managed limit env keys codex TOML config string (with model_context_window = __DEFAULT_MODEL_CONTEXT__) + auth.OPENAI_API_KEY + modelCatalog with {"__MODELS_CATALOG__": null} cc-switch stores a TOML doc, not env keys; no output knob exists; v3 adds the modelCatalog block so cc-switch emits Codex's model_catalog_json + a generated catalog file (Codex has no model discovery, so the catalog is the only way its picker learns our models) and drops the dead disable_response_storage key Codex 0.165.0 warns about gemini env with GEMINI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL, GEMINI_MODEL writer drops env keys outside its allow-list, so no limit fields open-code npm, options.baseURL/apiKey, {"__MODELS_OBJECT_LIMIT__": null} models as {id:{name,limit:{context,output}}} hermes snake_case base_url/api_key/api_mode, ["__MODELS_ARRAY_CTX_SNAKE__"] models as [{id,name,context_length}] open-claw flat baseUrl/apiKey, ["__MODELS_ARRAY_CTX__"] rejects npm/options as legacy keys; ≥1 model required; per-model contextWindow pi flat baseUrl (per-provider), ["__MODELS_ARRAY_CTX__"] pi reads the provider-level flat baseUrl; per-model contextWindow

Sizing note: each cc-switch archive is ~8-9 MB; the four-target matrix is ~35 MB. Far smaller than the retired uv + wheelhouse + python tiers.

docs.title: What we deliberately do NOT mirror
docs.text:
• Homebrew (packaging/homebrew/lite.rb) — a macOS developer behind the firewall can use /install the same as anyone else; brew taps imply external fetches.
  • npm, cargo, or any other toolchain — out of scope; the coding harnesses themselves (Claude Code, OpenCode, ...) are installed by the user through their own channels, and cc-switch writes their config. Mirroring those installers is a possible later extension, explicitly deferred (open-questions.md).

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
Almost everything is settled after the v4 review. What remains is small, and each item has a default so the plan is actionable without waiting.

Settled across v1-v4 (removed from the list):

  • Where artifacts are served from -> inside the gateway as a slice.
  • Storage backend -> RustFS, cluster-internal (v3's PVC was replaced in v4; the originally sketched MinIO was replaced by RustFS after MinIO Community Edition reached end of life).
  • How the store is filled -> admin REST sync API (slice talks to RustFS).
  • Harness auto-selection -> dropped; detection is a reporter.
  • Public path prefix -> everything under /install.
  • Wheelhouse form -> flat --find-links + --no-index; one version only.
  • Manifest signing -> not signing; master key is the trust anchor.
  • Harness mirroring -> non-goal; users install their own harnesses.
  • Upstream contribution -> none; proprietary jya0- branches only.
  • CLI version policy -> always equal to the gateway version.
  • Multi-replica storage -> resolved by RustFS being shared.
  • /install authentication -> unauthenticated.
  • Admin sync storage -> RustFS via the slice, master-key auth.

docs.title: 1. Windows native support timing
docs.text:
Git Bash / WSL is supported now (decision 4). Native /install.ps1 is deferred until a Windows user exists behind the firewall.

Default: Git Bash / WSL only; build /install.ps1 on demand.

docs.title: 2. Admin sync API authorization scope
docs.text:
The admin API uses _require_admin (PROXY_ADMIN), satisfied by the master key. If a non-master admin key should also sync artifacts (e.g. a CI key), decide whether that stays PROXY_ADMIN or becomes a narrower role.

Default: PROXY_ADMIN only, matching the oicm_routes.py precedent.

docs.title: 3. Spend-log archival cutover to RustFS
docs.text:
RustFS is now deployed and the litellm-logs bucket is planned for the S3 logging callback (s3_callback_params). Whether to actually switch spend-log archival to it (vs. the existing PVC-based janitor) is a separate, later decision; this design only reserves the bucket and the shared client.

Default: reserve the bucket now; migrate archival when the existing janitor's retention story needs revisiting.

docs.title: 4. One-previous retention window
docs.text:
The race guard keeps the outgoing version set briefly during a swap. How briefly (hours vs days) is an operational choice.

Default: keep the previous set until the next sync, then prune.

docs.title: Supported Platform Matrix
docs.text: cc-switch ships static binaries, so the matrix is small. We guarantee the targets below and label everything else honestly.

docs.title: Guaranteed (the mirror ships these)
docs.text:
Target Archive Covers Linux x86-64 musl cc-switch-cli-linux-x64-musl.tar.gz any Linux x86-64, glibc or musl (static) Linux ARM64 musl cc-switch-cli-linux-arm64-musl.tar.gz any Linux ARM64 macOS universal cc-switch-cli-darwin-universal.tar.gz Intel + Apple Silicon in one archive Windows x64 cc-switch-cli-windows-x64.zip via Git Bash / WSL

Static musl builds mean we do not need separate glibc/musl rows, and the macOS universal archive collapses the two Apple arches. Four artifacts cover the whole supported set.

docs.title: Supported on request (add to the manifest when needed)
docs.text: Target Archive Notes Linux x86-64 glibc cc-switch-cli-linux-x64.tar.gz only if a static-musl issue ever shows up Linux ARM64 glibc cc-switch-cli-linux-arm64.tar.gz same macOS arch-specific cc-switch-cli-darwin-{x64,arm64}.tar.gz smaller than universal; rarely needed

docs.title: Explicitly not promised
docs.text: Environment Why Windows ARM64 no upstream cc-switch artifact Android / Termux no upstream cc-switch artifact iOS / iPadOS not a sensible local CLI host; SSH into a Linux box instead FreeBSD no upstream cc-switch artifact

docs.title: What the guarantee means operationally
docs.text:
The mirror only ships artifacts for the guaranteed list (mirror-content.md); the install script refuses with a clear message on anything else rather than half-working. The manifest is the enforcement point: a platform not in cc_switch_artifacts is not installable. The matrix is re-checked whenever the pinned cc_switch_version moves.

The coding harnesses themselves (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, ...) are installed by the user through their own channels and have their own platform requirements; cc-switch only writes their config, it does not install them.

docs.title: Phase 0 — proof (half a day)
docs.text:
Goal: prove the mirror chain works on a clean network-isolated environment before any cluster changes.

  • Run the sync job on the workstation; produce the store locally (cc-switch archives + checksums + manifest + provider preset).
  • Serve it on localhost:8000 (python http.server or nginx).
  • Run the modified /install with the gateway URL pointed at localhost, inside a fresh container (docker run -it --network none after seeding the store, or a network namespace limited to localhost) — the point is that with GitHub/PyPI unroutable, the install still completes.
  • Success: cc-switch --version prints, the provider registers, cc-switch use <id> --app open-code writes ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, and a proxy that fails closed (HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1) shows zero external requests.

Phase 0 tests the script template + mirror content. In v4 that means the generator (unit tested: render with a known manifest, assert the origin overrides) and the bucket tree served locally. The two only meet in Phase 1.

docs.title: Phase 1 — pilot (1 week)
docs.text:
• Deploy RustFS + buckets, add the gateway env vars, and roll out the image that includes the slice wiring (per deployment.md); the admin then syncs artifacts via the API.
  • 2-3 pilot users on Linux x86-64; each does the full journey: /install -> paste gateway key -> pick harness(es) -> a day of real coding-agent use through their configured harness.
  • Watch: install success rate, the /v1/models key diagnostic (clear error on a wrong key), the harness multi-select UX, and whether the written harness config files (opencode.json, settings.json, config.toml) look right and are 0600. Also watch gateway metrics during a few parallel installs for any artifact-traffic impact on /v1 latency (expected none; the proxy streams from RustFS).
  • Resync check: add/remove a model on the gateway, re-run /install on a pilot machine, confirm the provider's model list updates and the run is otherwise a no-op.
  • Exit criteria: all pilots install without manual intervention and complete a real task through their agent; drop-detection tests green in CI.

docs.title: Phase 2 — general availability
docs.text:
• Announce with the single-command story (curl ... /install | sh, then paste your gateway key and pick your harnesses), plus the two-step cautious form from security.md.
  • State the update policy plainly: /install is the authoritative way to update cc-switch and re-sync models; do not run cc-switch update (it points at public GitHub, which the firewall blocks anyway).
  • Add a docs page under usage-guides once the flow is stable (deferred until then; this folder is the plan of record).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Where they come from: no new instrumentation needed —

  • Install/update health: the slice can log each /install/* GET (standard access logging); artifact download counts come from the same logs. Being in-app also means future metrics can join artifact downloads to real proxy telemetry if we ever care.
  • Usage: existing proxy telemetry (requests per virtual key, model distribution) already shows which keys are being used by CLI-driven agents.
  • CLI-side: lite itself reports its version in --version; a future lite doctor-style health check is an upstream feature, not ours.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
• Comment the wiring line (or drop the slice from the image) -> /install/* 404s; nothing else in the gateway is affected. The drop-detection tests intentionally fail in this state, which is the designed tripwire.
  • Installed clients keep working: lite talks only to /v1; a client whose mirror disappears is fully functional, it just cannot update.
  • Store rollback: republish the previous manifest (the race-guard retention keeps it briefly); the next /install run pins users to the older version.

docs.title: RustFS (Object Storage Backend)
docs.text: The artifact store and (later) spend-log archival both live in a single RustFS instance in the adeo-litellm namespace. This doc covers the deployment, the buckets, and the one shared S3 client so nothing is duplicated.

docs.title: Why RustFS, and why not MinIO
docs.text:
v3 chose a PVC. v4 moved to object storage for two reasons: it removes the multi-replica problem entirely (object storage is shared by nature, so the gateway can scale out without an RWX PVC or baked-in artifacts), and it earns its keep twice because LiteLLM already ships S3 logging support (integrations/s3.py, integrations/s3_v2.py) that currently points at nothing. One store, two tenants.

The backend is RustFS, not MinIO. MinIO Community Edition is end of life: the minio/minio repository was archived read-only in April 2026, and the Docker Hub images were deleted in September 2026 with quay.io closed to anonymous pulls, so there is no pullable minio/minio at any version. RustFS is an Apache-2.0, actively maintained, S3-compatible object store written in Rust, and S3 compatibility is the only contract anything in this design depends on: LiteLLM's logging path builds a stock boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url=...) (litellm/integrations/s3.py:74) and the v2 path hand-rolls SigV4 over raw HTTP against {endpoint}/{bucket}/{key}. Neither has any MinIO-specific code, so the swap is an endpoint and credential change, not a design change.

The pinned image, mirrored into the internal Harbor (public rustfs project):

registry.adeoaiengine.ecouncil.ae/rustfs/rustfs:1.0.1
sha256:38fcb422c93174dada595d1aedec0e942a16a2a01a0ecca896c4a563e1f463b5

docs.title: Buckets
docs.text:
Bucket Tenant Contents litellm-client-mirror the client-distribution slice cc-switch archives, manifest.json, providers/adeo/*/v<N>.json presets, templates/install.sh.tmpl litellm-logs LiteLLM's S3 logging callback (later) spend logs / audit logs, via s3_callback_params

Two buckets, not two RustFS instances. A separate mc alias or a separate bucket path is all the isolation needed; both tenants talk to the same endpoint with the same client code.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deployed in adeo-litellm alongside the gateway, Redis, and Postgres:

  • Single-node RustFS (StatefulSet + PVC) is sufficient for this workload; it is internal, low-throughput, and not a system of record for anything the cluster cannot regenerate (artifacts can be re-pushed, logs are archival).
  • Service rustfs.adeo-litellm.svc.cluster.local:9000 (S3 API).
  • Credentials in a litellm-rustfs-credentials Secret (access-key, secret-key), referenced by both tenants via secretKeyRef. Never in a ConfigMap, never committed. RustFS reads them as RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY / RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY.
  • No ingress for RustFS itself. It is cluster-internal; the gateway is the only thing that reaches it, and it reaches it over the cluster network. The dev machine never talks to RustFS directly (that is the whole point of the gateway proxy).
  • A NetworkPolicy allowing ingress only from the gateway pods (prod and dev labels) plus the bootstrap Job.
  • Runtime contract, verified by running the pinned image: non-root 10001:10001, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true with only /data mounted, no writable /tmp needed, console disabled, probes /health (liveness) and /health/ready (readiness), and RUSTFS_OBS_LOG_DIRECTORY set explicitly empty because the image bakes RUSTFS_OBS_LOG_DIRECTORY=/logs and telemetry initialization fails fatally when it cannot create it.
  • The data PVC uses the existing longhorn-crypto-global StorageClass (encrypted, Delete reclaim). No StorageClass is created by this deployment; the class is referenced by name. It was chosen over the cluster default longhorn-crypto-retain so a deleted StatefulSet does not leak its volume.
  • One store per environment, not shared. Dev and prod live in the same adeo-litellm namespace, so a single store would let a dev sync write prod's buckets. Dev runs rustfs-dev (own StatefulSet, PVC, credentials litellm-rustfs-credentials-dev, buckets litellm-client-mirror-dev and litellm-logs-dev, and a rustfs-dev NetworkPolicy admitting only the dev gateway and the dev store's pods); prod runs the symmetric unsuffixed set. The base is prod's store, the dev overlay renames, re-labels, and re-keys it via replacements (a labels transformer cannot be used: it would rewrite the NetworkPolicy's from selector and break the allow rule). The parity test pins that the two stay genuinely separate.

Bucket creation: a one-shot Job at bootstrap creates both buckets with the mc client (Harbor's registry.adeoaiengine.ecouncil.ae/minio/mc:latest, sha256:512a1cb685940ded1b0ff55470a226a3830e16305a3e0f1bfbb77056171601fd), which works unchanged against RustFS. RustFS has no MINIO_DEFAULT_BUCKETS-style startup hook, so the Job is required. It is idempotent: mc mb --ignore-existing succeeds on an existing bucket, and RustFS's own duplicate-bucket response is success rather than error. The Job pins runAsUser: 65532 (the mc image runs as root by default, which would trip runAsNonRoot) and carries ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 so a completed run reaps itself, matching the repo's other Jobs.

docs.title: The DRY S3 client
docs.text:
Both tenants use S3. Rather than two hand-rolled boto3 clients, there is one shared client factory, and both the logging callback and the slice read their parameters through it.

The upstream logging path already does exactly this pattern: litellm/integrations/s3.py builds its client from litellm.s3_callback_params (reading s3_endpoint_url, s3_bucket_name, the credential keys, and os.environ/... indirection for secrets — verified in the source). We reuse that, not replace it:

  • Logging tenant: config only, no code. Add s3_callback_params to the gateway's litellm_settings with s3_bucket_name: litellm-logs, s3_endpoint_url: os.environ/RUSTFS_ENDPOINT_URL, and the credential keys pointing at the Secret-backed env vars. LiteLLM's existing S3Logger does the rest. This is the "add that file syncing logic in a DRY manner" answer for logs: it is already written upstream, we just configure it.
  • Mirror tenant: the slice's admin API writes objects and the public route reads them. It uses the same s3_endpoint_url / bucket / credential parameters, sourced from the same env vars, through a thin shared helper so the slice does not re-declare them. If the helper and the callback ever disagree, the shared env var is the single source of truth.

Concretely, one set of env vars in the gateway Deployment feeds both:

RUSTFS_ENDPOINT_URL   -> http://rustfs.adeo-litellm.svc.cluster.local:9000
RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY     -> from litellm-rustfs-credentials
RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY     -> from litellm-rustfs-credentials

and the two tenants reference them by name. The slice's helper and the s3_callback_params both read those names, so there is one place to change the endpoint or credentials.

docs.title: What the slice does NOT do
docs.text: It does not implement object-storage semantics. Put/get/list/delete are RustFS's, via boto3 (already a litellm dependency, boto3>=1.43.1), using SigV4 with path-style addressing. The slice only adds the auth boundary (master key), the path containment, the hashing, and the manifest consistency check — the parts RustFS cannot do for us. That is the resolution of the v3 conflict: the admin does not point mc at RustFS directly (which would desync the manifest/DTO shape), it calls the slice, and the slice talks to RustFS.

docs.title: Failure behaviour
docs.text:
RustFS down must not take the gateway with it, same rule as every other dependency here:

  • The slice's public reads return 503 (or 404 for a missing object) when RustFS is unreachable; the gateway still boots and /v1 still serves.
  • The admin API returns 503; the admin retries the idempotent push loop.
  • The logging tenant: if s3_callback_params points at a down RustFS, LiteLLM's own callback error handling applies (it is a logging path, not the request path), so requests are unaffected.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Assets: developer machines (the script runs as the user, writes ~/.local/bin and harness config dirs like ~/.config/opencode and ~/.cc-switch), and the artifact store's integrity (what a compromised store could push to developers).

Trust anchors: TLS to litellm.ecouncil.ae (the firewall already requires this hostname; the cert serving is the existing DigiCert *.ecouncil.ae secret), RustFS's cluster-internal isolation, and the manifest's hashes.

docs.title: What lives where (the trust split)
docs.text:
The single most important security property of this design: executable bootstrap logic and mutable data are in different trust domains.

Gateway image / git (code review required to change):
  baked-in install template   <- the fallback script
  installer rendering logic

RustFS (admin-channel write authority required to change):
  templates/install.sh.tmpl       <- the live template, admin-synced
  cc-switch/<version>/<archives>  <- immutable, versioned
  manifest.json                   <- versioned, ETag/compare-and-swap

The install template is served from RustFS when a store copy exists, and the baked-in copy is the fallback when the store copy is missing or unreadable. This is a deliberate choice for iteration speed: tuning the install flow should not need a gateway image rebuild each time. The guardrail is that the store write path (PUT /install/admin/v1/artifact/templates/ install.sh.tmpl) is gated by the same PROXY_ADMIN check as every other artifact write — only an admin key can change the template, the same authority that can publish artifacts and the manifest. A non-admin bucket credential alone is not enough to reach it through the API.

The residual risk is accepted knowingly: an admin key holder can change the shell developers execute. That is already true of the artifacts + manifest the same key publishes, so the template does not widen the admin's existing authority. If template writes are ever delegated to a narrower role, the template should move back into the image at that point.

docs.title: Why /install and the artifact reads are unauthenticated (decision 9)
docs.text:
• The script and the artifacts contain no secrets: no API keys, no credentials. Downloading the binary needs no identity.
  • The user supplies their gateway virtual key when the script prompts for it (hidden input), which is where it belongs; the install path never logs or echoes it.
  • Personalization-by-key was considered and rejected: a plain curl of a static path carries no caller identity, and asking a user to pass a key to a piped shell would put secrets into shell history and process lists. The key is passed to cc-switch only via a --config-file written under umask 077, never as a command-line argument (argv is world-readable via /proc).

What unauthenticated does allow: anyone inside the network can download the CLI. Same posture as every internal tool's docs page, and the CLI without a key is useless. Rate-limiting is a cheap add if abuse ever shows up.

RustFS itself is not exposed: no ingress, and a NetworkPolicy allows only the gateway. The dev machine never talks to RustFS; it only ever reaches the gateway, which proxies the bytes.

docs.title: Write surface
docs.text:
The admin sync API (/install/admin/v1/*, see admin-sync.md) is the one authenticated surface. Its security properties:

  • Admin-only. Depends(user_api_key_auth) plus _require_admin (PROXY_ADMIN), the same pattern as litellm/proxy/oicm_routes.py. The master key satisfies it; a non-admin virtual key gets 403.
  • Prefix containment. Every artifact key is normalized against the litellm-client-mirror bucket prefix; .. and escapes are rejected, so the write API cannot reach the litellm-logs bucket or any other key.
  • Body size cap. A per-request limit (reject 413 above it) so a runaway client cannot fill the bucket in one request.
  • Manifest integrity. The manifest PUT verifies every referenced object exists with a matching hash and rejects 409 otherwise, so a published manifest never lies about the store.
  • Separate prefix. Write (/install/admin/*) and read (the rest of /install/*) are distinct sub-paths, so the ingress can restrict the write surface to an admin network range without affecting public reads.

The master key never appears in a tracked file: it lives in the litellm-master-key Secret and is supplied to the admin sync script from the environment, never committed. RustFS credentials likewise live only in the litellm-rustfs-credentials Secret, referenced by secretKeyRef.

docs.title: Integrity chain
docs.text:
1. The install script fetches /install/manifest.json first, over the same TLS. The manifest's SHA-256 values are the client-side source of truth.
  2. At ingest time the admin sync downloads each archive and verifies it against upstream's checksums.txt; only the verified hash goes into the manifest. The client never sees upstream's checksums file.
  3. The script verifies each downloaded archive against the manifest hash before extracting.
  4. The key the script writes into harness configs is the user's own gateway virtual key, validated against /v1/models before any file is touched.

Residual risk: the manifest itself. A store compromise can rewrite the manifest and the binaries together, so hash-checking is tamper-evidence against accidental corruption, not against a full store compromise. The bootstrap script is out of the store's reach (baked in the image), which is the property that bounds the blast radius: a store attacker can at worst deny service or serve a hash-mismatched binary (both detected), not inject shell.

docs.title: No manifest signing (decision 3)
docs.text:
Signing was dropped deliberately. The reasoning: the sole writer is a master-key-authenticated admin, so an attacker who can rewrite the manifest already holds the master key and has bigger problems. The sha256 hashes stay, because they still do work — corruption detection and the idempotency check on the write path. Dropping the signature drops the signature, not the hashes.

If the store ever becomes externally reachable, revisit; the in-app slice makes adding verification cheap (public key rides the image, the generator emits the verify step). Ed25519 signing of manifest.json at admin-sync time is the natural upgrade if that day comes.

docs.title: Client-side credential state
docs.text:
credentials land in two places, both user-owned and permission-checked:

  • cc-switch state at ~/.cc-switch/cc-switch.db. cc-switch v5.11.1 writes ~/.cc-switch as 0700 and the db as 0600 (verified; the earlier permissive-mode report, cc-switch-cli issue #212, is closed).
  • harness-native configs it writes (~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, ...). E2E asserts these are 0600.

The master/admin key never enters any of this: it authorizes only the /install/admin/* write surface and is never typed into the installer.

docs.title: cc-switch self-update is out of band
docs.text: cc-switch has its own update command that resolves the public GitHub releases — unreachable by design in this environment, and a bypass of our mirror if it were reachable. Policy: /install is the authoritative update mechanism; users do not run cc-switch update. There is no --source override on the command (verified v5.11.1), so this is enforced by documentation + the firewall, not config.

docs.title: Notes on the piped-curl pattern
docs.text:
curl | sh is normally an anti-pattern. Here it is acceptable because the script is ours, baked into a versioned gateway image, served over the same TLS as the API, and it hash-pins the binary via the manifest. The docs still offer the two-step form for cautious users:

curl -fsSL https://litellm.ecouncil.ae/install -o install.sh
less install.sh
sh install.sh

docs.title: Supply-chain hygiene for the admin sync script
docs.text: From the repo's CI supply-chain rules, applied to the fetch step: download to file + verify SHA-256 before use; pin every external tool by exact version and full URL; prefer official .sha256 sidecars (the cc-switch release publishes checksums.txt) over third-party checksum pages.

docs.title: Same-Origin Client Distribution — Design Plan
docs.text:
Status: design, not implemented. This folder is the plan of record for serving the LiteLLM CLI (lite) and its install chain from the OICM gateway, so a locked-down developer machine whose only reachable host is litellm.ecouncil.ae can go from bare OS to a configured coding agent with one command and zero external network access.

Everything here is designed against the current source tree (jya0-v1.102.0) and reuses existing upstream components wherever they exist.

docs.title: Revision note (v2)
docs.text: The first draft put the artifacts on a separate static-serving pod routed by nginx path. Review rejected that as overengineering: the gateway already serves its own Admin UI via StaticFiles and OICM custom routes via an APIRouter slice, so the same-origin chain now lives inside the running litellm gateway as a vertical slice (litellm/proxy/client_distribution/), pinned by the standard drop-detection tests. One deployment, one ingress rule, and /install becomes a generated artifact that can read the gateway's own state (config, DB, request host). See architecture.md for the decision record.

docs.title: Revision note (v4)
docs.text:
Ten review decisions folded in. The ones that changed the design:

  1. Everything under /install. One prefix for the user and the firewall. Public reads (/install/uv/..., /install/pypi/..., /install/python/..., /install/manifest.json) and the admin write surface (/install/admin/*) all nest under it.
  2. Only the latest uv and the latest lite. One current version set, with one previous retained purely as a race guard during a version swap.
  3. No manifest signing. The only writer is a master-key holder, so the key is already the trust anchor. Sha256 hashes stay (they do corruption detection and power the idempotency check).
  4. Windows via Git Bash / WSL now, native /install.ps1 deferred. The script's detection maps MINGW/MSYS to the Windows artifacts.
  5. No harness mirroring. Explicit non-goal: lite wires up a harness, it never installs one.
  6. No upstream contribution. Proprietary, jya0- branches only. This raises the importance of the drop-detection tests, since we maintain the fork ourselves.
  7. CLI version tracks the gateway version. Every gateway bump re-pins the litellm[cli] wheel to the same version number.
  8. Object storage replaces the PVC. Removes the multi-replica problem entirely and earns its keep twice (artifacts + the S3 logging path that already exists). The backend is RustFS, not MinIO, because MinIO Community Edition reached end of life (repository archived April 2026, Docker Hub images deleted September 2026); RustFS is S3-compatible, which is the only contract LiteLLM depends on. See rustfs.md.
  9. /install is unauthenticated. Downloading the binary and reading the manifest need no credential; the user supplies their admin-issued key when the script prompts for it (used for a /v1/models diagnostic and the provider's apiKey field).
  10. Admin uses the master key; the slice talks to RustFS on its behalf. The admin never points mc at RustFS directly, which would desync the manifest/DTO shape.

docs.title: Revision note (v3)
docs.text:
Three decisions from review, folded in:

  1. Storage is a PVC, not MinIO/S3. LiteLLM has S3 support but only as a logging callback (integrations/s3.py, s3_v2.py write spend/audit logs to a bucket via put_object; there is no serve/download path). Using object storage purely to hold a few CLI artifacts, when nothing else uses it beyond logs, is overkill. A PVC keeps it simple and matches the repo's existing PVC + CronJob patterns. See mirror-content.md and deployment.md.
  2. Admin-facing sync API on the gateway. Because a PVC can be deleted accidentally, the slice exposes admin-authenticated CRUD routes so an admin with internet access can push, upsert, or delete artifacts over REST, idempotently, using the gateway's master key as the bearer token. This replaces "admin copies bytes with kubectl cp" with a documented API. See admin-sync.md.
  3. Harness wiring lives in cc-switch, not the install script. The script installs cc-switch-cli and delegates provider registration and per-harness config-file writing to it. cc-switch supports 7 harnesses and writes each one's native config (including ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json), which the retired lite CLI never did for opencode/pi. See installer-script.md.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Developer machines inside the firewall can reach litellm.ecouncil.ae (443) and nothing else. The upstream lite install flow assumes unrestricted egress:

raw.githubusercontent.com -> install-cli.sh
astral.sh                 -> uv installer
github.com                -> uv release tarballs (via the installer)
PyPI                      -> litellm[cli] + dependencies
github.com                -> managed CPython (python-build-standalone, via uv)

Every hop except the first script itself is a blocked host, so the official installer fails on these machines after the first curl.

docs.title: Goal and non-goals
docs.text:
Goal: curl -fsSL https://litellm.ecouncil.ae/install | sh installs a working lite, and every subsequent network operation the CLI performs stays on litellm.ecouncil.ae. The end user never needs to know that uv, a wheelhouse, or a Python mirror exist.

Non-goals:

  • No fork of upstream litellm[cli]. All client behavior stays the stock CLI (lite configure, lite login, lite claude/codex/opencode/pi, model sync via /v1/models). We distribute; we do not modify. The only new code is the gateway-side serving slice.
  • No per-user personalized install scripts in v1. The served script is generic (with the gateway URL and adopted versions generated from gateway state); the per-key personalization already happens client-side at runtime (agent_model_sync_env fetches /v1/models with the user's key). The slice's in-app position makes authenticated/personalized variants a possible future extension — recorded, not built.
  • No new auth surface in v1. /install and the artifact routes are unauthenticated (see security.md for the reasoning and the bootstrap paradox).
  • No guarantee of literal universality. See platform-matrix.md for the supported matrix and the Android/iOS stance.

docs.title: Design in one paragraph
docs.text: Keep upstream's exact installation mechanism and move its origins. uv is the only piece of the chain that is a genuine standalone binary, so we mirror the pinned uv release artifacts; we mirror the litellm[cli] wheel closure as a flat wheelhouse; and we mirror the exact CPython builds uv would fetch. All of it lives in a cluster-internal RustFS bucket, and is served by a vertical slice inside the running gateway under a single /install prefix: the artifact reads proxy from RustFS, and GET /install is a router handler that generates the bootstrap script at request time, baking in the gateway's own base URL and the currently adopted versions from manifest.json. The script body is upstream's scripts/install-cli.sh with three origin changes (INSTALLER_DOWNLOAD_URL for the uv bootstrap, --no-index --find-links for the wheelhouse, UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_MIRROR for managed Python), then lite config set base_url pre-configures the CLI and the stock flow takes over. No modification of litellm's or uv's logic; one new slice, one wiring line, drop-detection tests.

docs.text:
Hooks are registered in the proxy config's litellm_settings.callbacks list. The deployed list lives in the litellm-config ConfigMap at deploy/base/gateway/config/litellm-config.yaml:

litellm_settings:
  callbacks:
    - litellm_hooks.vllm_param_injector.vllm_param_injector
    - dynamic_rate_limiter_v3_htb
    - litellm_hooks.priority_bridge.priority_bridge
    - prometheus
    - litellm.router_utils.session_identity.resolver.proxy_handler_instance

The two litellm_hooks.* names are mounted from the litellm-hooks ConfigMap (declared at deploy/base/shared/litellm-hooks.yaml) into /app/litellm_hooks on the proxy pod. dynamic_rate_limiter_v3_htb is a LiteLLM in-tree hook (see OICM Custom Code); prometheus and the session-identity resolver are in-tree too.

Note

keda_metrics.py is not in the litellm-hooks ConfigMap and not in the deployed callbacks list, so the ml_model_concurrent_requests gauge it defines is not currently emitted in prod. Register it in the ConfigMap and the callbacks list if KEDA autoscaling on that metric is needed again.

docs.title: Custom Providers
docs.text: This section documents the custom LLM providers integrated into the LiteLLM proxy for the OICM platform. Each provider has its own API surface, authentication scheme, and request/response shaping that differs from the standard OpenAI-compatible path.

docs.title: Inception
docs.text:
Inception Labs diffusion-based LLMs (Mercury series). Supports chat completions, text completions (FIM), text-to-speech, and speech-to-text. Uses OpenAI-compatible API shapes (/v1/audio/speech, /v1/audio/transcriptions, /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions) but requires custom handler dispatch in litellm/main.py because router-level kwargs (e.g. use_in_pass_through) must be stripped before the request reaches the upstream pod.

Key implementation files: - litellm/llms/inception/common_utils.py — InceptionAudioModelInfo, INCEPTION_INTERNAL_PARAMS - litellm/llms/inception/text_to_speech/transformation.py — InceptionTextToSpeechConfig - litellm/llms/inception/transcription/transformation.py — InceptionAudioTranscriptionConfig - litellm/llms/inception/chat/transformation.py — InceptionChatConfig - litellm/llms/inception/completion/transformation.py — InceptionTextCompletionConfig

docs.title: Hamsa
docs.text:
Hamsa Arabic/English TTS and STT with voice cloning and realtime WebSocket support. Uses a custom API surface (/tts/stream, /transcribe, /tts/voice_clone, /ws) with x-api-key header authentication. Not in openai_compatible_providers, so all endpoints use explicit provider branches in litellm/main.py.

docs.title: OmniVoice
docs.text:
OmniVoice is a k2-fsa OpenAI-compatible TTS server with one-shot voice cloning. Uses OpenAI-compatible API shapes (/v1/audio/speech) for standard TTS plus a multipart form-data endpoint (/v1/audio/speech/clone) for voice cloning. No API key required. In both openai_compatible_providers and _CUSTOM_AUDIO_HANDLER_PROVIDERS. The speech() function in litellm/main.py detects ref_audio in kwargs to switch between standard TTS (JSON body) and voice clone (multipart form-data) configs.

Key implementation files: - litellm/llms/omnivoice/common_utils.py — OmniVoiceModelInfo, OMNIVOICE_INTERNAL_PARAMS - litellm/llms/omnivoice/text_to_speech/transformation.py — OmniVoiceTextToSpeechConfig - litellm/llms/omnivoice/voice/transformation.py — OmniVoiceVoiceCloneConfig - litellm/proxy/voice_routes.py — audio_speech_clone route for /v1/audio/speech/clone - oicm-litellm-layer/controller/models.py — detect_provider() detects k2-fsa/k2fsa as omnivoice

docs.text: Diarization-only provider behind the POST /v1/diarize route, served by coro deployments and named for the pyannoteAI cloud contract it implements (coro is a tool wrapper; the provider is the contract). See PYANNOTE_DIARIZATION_PROVIDER_PLAN.md for the recorded choices and slice plan: multipart in / DiarizationJob JSON out, full 7-layer slice (controller-discovered api_base rules out pass-through), new diarization mode, per-field 400s passed through verbatim, no auth header injection. One serving id pyannote/community-1 end to end: client sends it, it is the registered model_name, the ADEO coro image bakes CORO_PYANNOTE_DIARIZE_MODEL_ID=pyannote/community-1 so the pod accepts and echoes it, and the controller registers pyannote/pyannote/community-1 (the double prefix is what makes the provider split land on the serving id).

docs.title: Capability registration: probe the deployment, don't trust the route table
docs.text:
Demoted to last-resort tier by CAPABILITY_REGISTRATION_REVIEW2.md. Verification found that OICM's deployment_summary already carries an inference_task declaration (HF-derived enum) that the controller's wire DTO silently drops. Declared task beats probing as the primary tier; the probe table survives as tier 2 for deployments that declare nothing. The three-verdict semantics and method-matched probing below remain correct and are the part worth keeping.

Supersedes the detection proposals in FISHAUDIO_DRAMA3_ROBUST_FIX_DESIGN.md. The framing there was wrong: it treated registration as a path-shape inference problem and proposed ever-better heuristics. The right framing is that a deployment's capability is a fact you can ask it for, and openapi.json is a poor proxy for that fact.

Parent direction: the gateway's only job is to serve registered models correctly. OICM and Kubernetes own deployment. So the controller's job is to register each deployment's capabilities accurately, not to hardcode if conditions that encode one vendor's path list.

docs.title: Why openapi.json is the wrong oracle
docs.text:
It reports what routes exist, not what the deployment can do. Three verified counterexamples on today's cluster:

Pod /v1/chat/completions in openapi Actually usable for chat Correct mode VibeVoice-ASR (vLLM) yes yes (POST returns 200) chat Drama 3 (sglang-omni) yes no (POST returns 400, "speech input must be text") audio_speech Qwen3-ASR (vLLM) — native transcription surface audio_transcription

All three are hosted_vllm-class pods. A path table cannot separate rows 1 and 2; that is why the current chat-first rule is correct for VibeVoice and wrong for Drama 3. No reordering of _PATH_MODES fixes that, and neither does any other static table, because the information is not in the path list.

docs.title: The distinction that does work: mounted vs. usable
docs.text:
Probing the live pods shows the servers distinguish two failures that the controller currently conflates:

Status Meaning Example 200 Surface works VibeVoice POST /v1/chat/completions with a text prompt 400 Surface is mounted, request rejected (bad body, wrong modality) Drama 3 POST /v1/chat/completions -> "the speech input must be text" 404/405 Surface not mounted (or unknown model id) Drama 3 POST /v1/embeddings, vLLM POST /v1/chat/completions with a bad model id

A 400 from a well-formed request means "this endpoint exists and inspects my payload" — i.e. mounted but not the deployment's capability. A 404 means "this deployment doesn't serve this surface at all". That difference is the capability signal, and it is exactly what probe_verdict_to_fact in controller/capabilities.py:91 was already built to classify: 200 -> accepts, content-refusal codes -> rejects, everything else -> unknown. The existing synthetic image/audio probes reuse this and are already memoized per deployment. The capability machinery is there; it is pointed at modalities, not modes.

Caveat found while validating: a GET-only pre-filter is not portable. vLLM answers GET /v1/chat/completions with 404 while happily serving POST, so mount detection must use the same method the capability would use. Probing GET to decide would misclassify real vLLM chat pods.

docs.title: Design: a capability probe table as data, with a declared override
docs.text: Three layers, in precedence order.

docs.title: 1. Declared override wins (operator intent)
docs.text:
Reuse the ConfigMap field mechanism the controller already has (local_deployments.py:122,173 reads MODEL_ID and EXTRA_ARGS). Add MODE:

MODE=audio_speech

This is for the cases where a human knows better than any probe: a pod that is temporarily unhealthy, a canary, a deployment whose intent is genuinely ambiguous. It is a data change, not a code change.

docs.title: 2. Probe table as data, not if conditions
docs.text:
The parent asked for a "better formatted json capability easy to edit list". Agreed, with one correction: the table should describe capability probes, not path-to-mode mappings, because the mapping is what keeps being wrong. Proposed shape, in controller/capabilities.py (or a sibling controller/probes.py), loaded from a YAML/JSON file the way exclusions.py and sources_config.py already do:

probes:
  - capability: chat
    method: POST
    path: /v1/chat/completions
    body: {model: "$MODEL_ID", messages: [{role: user, content: "hi"}], max_tokens: 1}
    success: 200
  - capability: audio_speech
    method: POST
    path: /v1/audio/speech
    body: {model: "$MODEL_ID", input: "hi", response_format: wav}
    success: 200
    discard_response: true     # audio is large; never buffer it
  - capability: audio_transcription
    method: POST
    path: /v1/audio/transcriptions
    multipart: file=$SYNTH_AUDIO
    success: 200
  - capability: diarization
    method: POST
    path: /v1/diarize
    ...

Then the rule becomes a single ordered reduction, not a table of special cases:

  • a capability whose probe succeeds (200) is available;
  • a capability whose probe is a content refusal (400/415/422) is mounted-but-unusable, so it must not win;
  • a capability that is unknown (404, timeout, 5xx) is not claimed.

Mode selection then walks the available set in declared priority (from the same file, e.g. [chat, audio_speech, audio_transcription, diarization, embeddings, rerank, ocr]), taking the first capability that succeeded. Drama 3: chat 400, speech 200 -> audio_speech. VibeVoice: chat 200 -> chat. Qwen3-ASR: transcription 200 -> audio_transcription. No vendor names in the code path.

Because the probe table is data, adding a new serving stack is a config change; the code only knows about success / refusal / unknown and the ordering rule.

docs.title: 3. Server family as a cheap hint, not the decider
docs.text:
The parent's instinct that sglang and vLLM are identifiable is right, and the image name is already available on the Deployment object (dep.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image), currently unused. Verified distinct: sglang:, sglang-omni:, adeo-vllm: in the registry path.

Use it to bound the probe set, not to determine the mode: an adeo-vllm/sglang image is known to serve the OpenAI family, so probe the standard set; an unknown image (custom fork, custom endpoint shapes) probes only what the declared table lists and otherwise defers to the ConfigMap. This keeps the fingerprint as an optimization and default, never as the source of truth — which is what makes it safe, since image names are not a contract and a custom fork can do anything.

Also note: sglang-omni answers /model_info, while plain sglang answers /get_server_info and 404s /model_info; adeo-vllm 404s both. So even "which metadata endpoint exists" already varies three ways. Another reason the capability has to be probed rather than inferred.

docs.title: Where custom providers fit
docs.text: Custom providers (hamsa, pyannote, omnivoice) remap a LiteLLM path to a pod-specific path. Under this design they stay exactly as they are: their pods fail the standard probes (so no standard capability is claimed), the ConfigMap MODE declares the intent, and detect_provider still picks the custom config by name. The probe table supplies the mode, the provider registry supplies the transport. Those are orthogonal, which is why no capability logic needs to know about them.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Measured live on the Drama 3 pod: a chat probe returning 400 takes ~326 ms; a minimal speech probe (~1 s of audio) takes ~537 ms; eight GET mount checks take ~2.6 s in total but are not method-safe (see caveat). Memoize per (uuid, image-digest) the way _synthetic_probe_cache already memoizes modalities, and the steady-state cost is one probe set per deployment redeploy. Stop probing a capability once it succeeds.

docs.title: Test strategy
docs.text: The probe_verdict_to_fact helper and its _CONTENT_REFUSAL_CODES set are the pivot, so pin them first. Then table-test the reduction: [chat=200, speech=400] -> chat; [chat=400, speech=200] -> audio_speech; [chat=404, speech=200] -> audio_speech; [chat=unknown] -> no claim, keep previous mode. The last case matters: an unreachable probe must never demote a working deployment.

docs.title: Summary of the change from the previous design
docs.text:
Previous This design Reorder _PATH_MODES Static path tables are the bug, not the fix; probe mutation ConfigMap MODE only ConfigMap stays, but as override, not the primary mechanism Serve-intent via supported_task_types Pods don't publish it; probe behavior instead Per-provider fishaudio slice Capability is orthogonal to provider; unchanged

The hosted_vllm TTS pass-through config from the previous document is still worth doing, and is now independent: that one fixes request field forwarding, this one fixes registration. They should not be bundled.

docs.title: Capability registration: review of the probe design, and the simpler answer the data already gives
docs.text: A second review of CAPABILITY_REGISTRATION_BY_PROBE.md, asked for by the parent. Verdict up front: the probe design is sound as a last-resort tier, but verification of what already flows through the controller found a declaration layer that makes most of the probing unnecessary. The probe table should be demoted from primary mechanism to tie-breaker. Three findings, in order of importance.

docs.title: Finding 1: OICM already declares the capability, and the controller drops it
docs.text:
The parent asked to reuse existing logic. There is more to reuse than expected: the deployment_summary payload the status poller already fetches every 10 seconds carries an inference_task field — OICM's own ModelServerTasks enum, derived from the HuggingFace task taxonomy — plus model_server_name and model_server_tag. The operator picked the task when deploying the model. It is the declaration of intent, arriving continuously, and OicmDeploymentSummary (controller/status/wire.py:85) throws it away because the field is simply not declared on the DTO.

Verified live on both sources (Al Ain 27 deployments, Abu Dhabi 1):

Deployment inference_task model_server_name fishaudio/drama-3 (51096511) Text-to-Speech None (custom_model_server image instead) microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR (061fbb9d) Automatic Speech Recognition vLLM Qwen3-Next, DeepSeek-V4-Flash Text Generation vLLM / SGLang Qwen3-Embedding-* Text Embedding vLLM Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1 Text-to-Image SGLang coro (d4398150, diarization) None (custom image path) None

The enum has 49 values including Diarization, Text Ranking, Question Answering. Both OICM versions (Al Ain 1.15.19 and AD 1.7.1) return it.

This is strictly better than my ConfigMap MODE proposal: same authority (the operator's deploy-time declaration), but no new mechanism to wire, no ConfigMap to edit per deployment, and it flows through plumbing that already exists and is already tested.

Design consequence: mode selection gains a first tier with zero new infrastructure:

tier 0: inference_task from deployment_summary     (declared, per-deployment)
tier 1: ConfigMap MODE override                    (escape hatch for tier-0 mistakes)
tier 2: capability probes                           (last resort when tier 0 is absent)
tier 3: path-shape detection                        (today's fallback, stays as the floor)

The mapping from ModelServerTasks to LiteLLM mode is a small static table in the controller, data not code — exactly the "better formatted json capability easy to edit list" the parent asked for, but populated from OICM instead of hand-maintained:

{
  "Text Generation": "chat",
  "Image-Text-to-Text": "chat",
  "Text-to-Speech": "audio_speech",
  "Automatic Speech Recognition": "audio_transcription",
  "Text Embedding": "embedding",
  "Text-to-Image": "image_generation",
  "Diarization": "diarization"
}

Unmapped tasks degrade to tier 2, never crash.

docs.title: The hole this closes that probing cannot
docs.text: Probes observe the surface; they cannot observe intent. VibeVoice-ASR is the standing example: POST /v1/chat/completions returns 200 there, so probing classifies it chat, while OICM says its task is Automatic Speech Recognition. Both are true — the capability is chat, the task is ASR. Under a probe-primary design the row reads chat and the ASR declaration is lost. Under tier-0-primary the row carries both facts: mode=chat (from the task mapping, see finding 3) and the raw task preserved for consumers. The declaration and the observation are different facts and the record should keep both.

docs.title: Finding 2: the probe design's holes, and what survives
docs.text:
Honest holes in CAPABILITY_REGISTRATION_BY_PROBE as written:

Cost under churn. Every _handle_add runs discovery, which would run the probe set. A pod that crash-loops repays the full probe cost on every restart, and probes are real inference (a TTS probe generates audio). Mitigation exists but must be explicit: memoize on (uuid, pod-spec image digest), and skip probes entirely when tier 0/1 already decided.

Probes mutate the deployment's state. sglang counts requests; a probe inflates its metrics, and a 400 from a TTS pod still writes a log line per probe. Individually trivial, multiplied by 300 s sync cycles and 27 deployments it is noise the platform team then has to filter. Mitigation: probe once per (uuid, digest) and stop once a capability is confirmed.

A 400 is not always a modality refusal. probe_verdict_to_fact treats 400 as rejection, but a pod can 400 for a malformed probe body (our bug) as easily as for a wrong modality (their state). If the probe table's body drifts from what the server accepts — say a max_tokens field the new server version rejects — every pod silently classifies as "not chat". Mitigation: a probe result must carry its evidence (the response snippet) into the log, and an unexpected-4xx rate above some threshold should page rather than silently demote 27 models.

Diarization's probing is awkward. coro accepts a multipart upload; a minimal probe needs a real audio file shipped in the probe table. That is fine, but it means the probe config format needs multipart support and an inline audio fixture, which is the most complex entry in the file by far.

The double-404 trap. vLLM answers 404 both for "route not mounted" and for "unknown model id" — verified live when my probe used a wrong model id. Any probe runner must read /v1/models first and substitute the real id, or the whole table misclassifies. This is a correctness requirement on the runner, not a design flaw, but it is the kind of detail that silently breaks.

What survives review: the three-verdict classification (200 works / content-refusal mounted-but-wrong-modality / unknown no-claim) is exactly right and probe_verdict_to_fact already implements it. The probe table as data survives. Method-matching (probe with the capability's own HTTP method) survives — the GET finding was correct and important.

docs.title: Finding 3: reuse the /endpoints status layer for the residual ambiguity
docs.text:
The parent asked what can be reused from the /api/v1/models/x/x/endpoints logic. Concretely reusable, verified:

GatewayStateResolver (gateway_status.py:132) is the pattern to copy, not the code to call. It maps one set of observed facts to one verdict with a documented decision record, keeps facts separate from presentation (serving_available separate from availability), and owns staleness as a first-class concern. The task-to-mode mapping should be built the same way: a frozen dataclass in, a GatewayStatus-style verdict out, staleness and unknown mapped to "claim nothing, keep the previous mode" — never a silent demotion. The controller's change-guard philosophy (_patch_is_noop only writes when a compared fact moved) is the write-amplification guard, already in reconciler.py.

supports_diarization in mapping/endpoints.py:142 shows the task belongs in model_info. It reads deployment.model_info.get("mode") == "diarization" today. Once tier 0 lands, the raw inference_task string should also be stamped into model_info.oicm_task so the public endpoint surface can key off the declaration instead of inferring from mode. That is a two-line change in _register_payload/patch_status and it makes the whole chain — OICM declaration to public API — inspectable end to end.

The oicm status block is the proven transport. model_info.oicm already flows (v, status, serving_available, replicas, observed_at) and StatusPersister already writes it with a change guard and heartbeat staleness. Adding inference_task to the wire DTO (wire.py:85), the snapshot (snapshot.py:28), and the persisted block is the same shape of change that added oicm_cluster — the memory notes record exactly this precedent.

docs.title: The VibeVoice resolution, concretely
docs.text:
With all four tiers, VibeVoice resolves correctly at every level:

  • tier 0: Automatic Speech Recognition maps toward audio_transcription
  • but the serving surface is chat, so the transport probe or path detection must be allowed to override toward chat when the native surface is not mounted

So the final rule is not "tier 0 wins, full stop". It is: tier 0 decides the task; the transport layer decides how to serve it; when they disagree, the disagreement is recorded, not silently resolved. Concretely: mode follows the mounted surface (VibeVoice ends chat, as today), and model_info.oicm_task preserves the declared ASR intent. The endpoints layer can then advertise "ASR served via chat" honestly instead of losing one of the two facts. This is the same facts-vs-presentation split GatewayStateResolver already models.

docs.title: Revised recommendation
docs.text:
Status (2026-11-03): steps 1 and 2 are shipped and running in prod. Steps 3 and 4 remain open. See Shipped state at the end of this document for what actually landed and what the live rows look like.

  1. Stop dropping inference_task. Add it to OicmDeploymentSummary + OicmStatusSnapshot + the persisted oicm block, and stamp model_info.oicm_task. Pure additive plumbing through tested code, fixes the data availability for everything downstream. Smallest possible first step.
  2. Task-to-mode mapping as data in the controller. A static table, degraded by tiers 1-3 where the task is absent or ambiguous. Fix Drama 3 by declaring, not probing.
  3. Keep the probe table as the last-resort tier only. For custom_model_server deployments whose task is None and whose ConfigMap carries no MODE (coro today registers correctly through path detection, so this tier exists for the next unknown pod).
  4. Path detection stays as the floor. It already handles Hamsa's native surface and OCR. Reordering _PATH_MODES (TTS before transcription) remains a small, correct fix.

This keeps the probe design's real contribution (the three-verdict semantics, method-matched probes, table-as-data) while making the declared task — the strongest, cheapest, already-flowing signal — the primary tier. The gateway keeps its single job: serve what the controller registered, with the mode and the task both in the row.

docs.title: Shipped state (2026-11-03)
docs.text: Both controllers run oicm-discovery-controller:0.1.0-20261103-4d922d8 in prod and dev, syncing 26-27 models per cycle.

docs.title: What landed
docs.text:
controller/models.py holds two tables, and one function consumes them:

Table Purpose _TASK_MODES inference_task → controller mode, 8 entries. Data, not code _TASK_SURFACE_PATHS The path that proves each task's native surface is mounted

detect_mode_from_task(task, paths) returns the task's mode only when that task's native surface path appears in the pod's probed openapi.json. Otherwise it returns None and discovery falls through to detect_mode_from_paths. That gate is what keeps VibeVoice on chat while letting Drama 3 become audio_speech, and a test (test_every_non_chat_task_has_a_surface_gate) fails if a non-chat task is ever added without a gate entry.

The declaration is preserved separately as model_info.oicm_task, written at registration, in the reconciler patch, and in the status write.

docs.title: Live rows, prod and dev identical
docs.text:
Model mode oicm_task Notes fishaudio/drama-3 audio_speech Text-to-Speech plus health_check_voice: default microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR chat Automatic Speech Recognition surface wins, declaration preserved Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1 image_generation Text-to-Image was chat before this work CohereLabs/cohere-transcribe-arabic-07-2026 audio_transcription Automatic Speech Recognition task and surface agree Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-* embedding Text Embedding chat models (13) chat Text Generation / Image-Text-to-Text

PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 declares Image-Text-to-Text and stays chat, which is the surface rule doing its job.

docs.title: The probe-voice stamp
docs.text: A task-declared TTS row also receives model_info.health_check_voice: "default". The gateway's audio_speech probe otherwise sends voice="alloy", which Drama 3 rejects with a 400. The stamp is scoped to non-native providers (OicmModel.health_check_stamp): hamsa resolves voice to a speaker name it validates, so it must keep the gateway default.

docs.title: Deployment notes
docs.text: Promote a dev-validated controller tag to prod without rebuilding: make controller-deploy-prod BUILD=0 TAG=<tag> (see Makefile reference).

docs.title: Still open
docs.text:
1. Tier 1, the ConfigMap MODE escape hatch. Not built. Today the only override is editing _TASK_MODES and redeploying.
  2. Tier 2, the probe table. Not built; CAPABILITY_REGISTRATION_BY_PROBE.md remains the design of record for it.
  3. _PATH_MODES ordering. TRANSCRIPTION_PATH still precedes TTS_PATH, so a path-detected pod serving both would resolve to audio_transcription. Tier 0 now covers the pods that matter (they declare their task), so this only bites a deployment that mounts both surfaces and declares nothing.
  4. Keyless TTS on hosted_vllm. Fixed in 87c91acdcc (speech() now prefers the provider-resolved dynamic_api_key), but not yet in a deployed image. Prod masks the bug because its Deployment sets HOSTED_VLLM_API_KEY; dev does not, so drama-3's dev health probe still reports AuthenticationError.
  5. rerank and the gateway's mode Literal. detect_mode_from_paths can emit "rerank", which ModelInfo.mode's Literal omits even though the health-check handlers support it. Type-level gap only.

docs.title: POST /v1/voices/profiles
docs.text:
Create a voice cloning profile from reference audio. The profile can later be used via voice: "clone:<profile_id>" in /v1/audio/speech.

  -F "ref_audio=@reference_audio.wav" \
  -F "ref_text=The text spoken in the reference audio." \
  -F "overwrite=true"

Form Parameters:

Parameter Type Required Default Description profile_id string Yes — Unique ID. Alphanumeric, dashes, underscores. Max 64 chars. ref_audio file Yes — Reference audio file (WAV/MP3/FLAC). Max 25MB. ref_text string No null Transcript of the reference audio. If omitted, Whisper ASR auto-transcribes at synthesis time. overwrite bool No false Overwrite if profile already exists.

Content-Type: application/json

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "omnivoice",
    "input": "Hello, this is a test of the OmniVoice text-to-speech system.",

docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "omnivoice",
    "input": "This uses a stored clone profile for voice cloning.",

docs.title: Streaming (PCM chunks)
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "omnivoice",
    "input": "This is a longer text that will be streamed in chunks. Each sentence is synthesized and sent as soon as it is ready.",
    "stream": true,
    "response_format": "pcm",
    "position_temperature": 0.0
  }' \
  --output output.pcm

Streaming requires response_format: "pcm". Set position_temperature: 0.0 for consistent voice across chunks. Convert to WAV afterwards: ffmpeg -f s16le -ar 24000 -ac 1 -i output.pcm output.wav

docs.title: Advanced generation parameters
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "omnivoice",
    "input": "This synthesis uses advanced generation parameters for quality tuning.",
    "instructions": "female,american accent",
    "num_step": 32,
    "guidance_scale": 3.5,
    "position_temperature": 0.0,
    "layer_penalty_factor": 0.5,
    "response_format": "wav"
  }' \
  --output output.wav

Request Body:

Parameter Type Required Default Range Description model string No "omnivoice" omnivoice, tts-1, tts-1-hd Model alias (all map to same engine) input string Yes — 1–10,000 chars Text to synthesize voice string No "auto" SeeVoice Reference Voice selector: preset name,clone:<id>, design:<attrs>, or auto instructions string No null Design attributes Voice design attributes (e.g."female,british accent") response_format string No "wav" mp3, opus, aac, flac, wav, pcm Output audio format speed float No 1.0 0.25–4.0 Speech speed multiplier stream bool No false — Enable sentence-level PCM streaming num_step int No 32 (server default) 1–64 Diffusion steps. Higher = better quality, slower. guidance_scale float No server default 0.0–10.0 CFG scale. Higher = stronger voice conditioning. denoise bool No server default — Enable upstream denoising token t_shift float No server default 0.0–2.0 Noise schedule shift position_temperature float No server default 0.0–10.0 Temperature for mask-position selection. 0 = deterministic. class_temperature float No server default 0.0–2.0 Temperature for token sampling. 0 = greedy. duration float No null 0.1–60.0 Target audio duration in seconds language string No null Language code Language code (e.g."en", "vi", "zh") for multilingual pronunciation layer_penalty_factor float No null ≥0.0 Layer penalty factor for quality tuning preprocess_prompt bool No null — Preprocess the input prompt postprocess_output bool No null — Postprocess the output audio request_timeout_s int No server default 1–600 Per-request timeout in seconds

Response Headers:

Header Description X-Audio-Duration-S Generated audio duration in seconds X-Synthesis-Latency-S Total model inference latency in seconds

Response Body: Binary audio data in the requested format.

docs.title: POST /v1/audio/speech/clone
docs.text:
One-shot voice cloning. Upload reference audio directly — no profile needed.

Content-Type: multipart/form-data

docs.title: With reference text (fast — no Whisper needed)
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech/clone \
  -F "text=This is one-shot voice cloning without saving a profile." \
  -F "ref_audio=@reference_audio.wav" \
  -F "ref_text=The text spoken in the reference audio." \
  -F "speed=1.0" \
  --output output.wav

docs.title: Without reference text (slower — Whisper ASR auto-transcribes)
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech/clone \
  -F "text=This is voice cloning with automatic transcription." \
  -F "ref_audio=@reference_audio.wav" \
  -F "speed=1.0" \
  --output output.wav

When ref_text is omitted, the server uses Whisper ASR to transcribe the reference audio automatically. This adds ~0.3–0.5s latency.

docs.title: Streaming clone
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/speech/clone \
  -F "text=Long text to be streamed in sentence-level chunks..." \
  -F "ref_audio=@reference_audio.wav" \
  -F "ref_text=Reference text." \
  -F "stream=true" \
  -F "response_format=pcm" \
  --output output.pcm

Form Parameters:

Parameter Type Required Default Range Description text string Yes — 1–10,000 chars Text to synthesize ref_audio file Yes — Max 25MB Reference audio file ref_text string No null — Transcript of reference audio. If omitted, Whisper ASR auto-transcribes. response_format string No "wav" mp3, opus, aac, flac, wav, pcm Output audio format stream bool No false — Enable sentence-level PCM streaming speed float No 1.0 0.25–4.0 Speech speed multiplier num_step int No server default 1–64 Diffusion steps guidance_scale float No server default 0.0–10.0 CFG scale language string No null Language code Language for multilingual pronunciation duration float No null 0.1–60.0 Target audio duration in seconds request_timeout_s int No server default 1–600 Per-request timeout

Advanced parameters (denoise, t_shift, position_temperature, class_temperature, layer_penalty_factor, preprocess_prompt, postprocess_output, audio_chunk_duration, audio_chunk_threshold) are also accepted — see POST /v1/audio/speech for details.

Response: Same as /v1/audio/speech — binary audio with X-Audio-Duration-S and X-Synthesis-Latency-S headers.

docs.title: POST /v1/audio/script
docs.text:
Multi-speaker script synthesis with voice resolution, pause insertion, and error handling.

Content-Type: application/json

docs.title: Single-track output (mixed WAV)
docs.text:
Produces a single mixed audio file with pauses between speaker changes.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/script \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "script": [
      {"speaker": "narrator", "text": "Welcome to the OmniVoice script synthesis demo.", "voice": "openai:onyx"},
      {"speaker": "alice", "text": "Hello! I am Alice, and I will be your guide today.", "voice": "openai:nova"},
      {"speaker": "narrator", "text": "Thank you Alice. Let us begin.", "voice": "openai:onyx"}
    ],
    "default_voice": "openai:onyx",
    "speed": 1.0,
    "on_error": "abort",
    "pause_between_speakers": 0.3,
    "response_format": "wav",
    "output_format": "single_track"
  }' \
  --output script.wav

docs.title: Multi-track output (per-speaker WAV, base64-encoded JSON)
docs.text:
Returns each speaker's audio as a separate base64-encoded WAV track with segment timestamps.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/script \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "script": [
      {"speaker": "narrator", "text": "Welcome to the demo.", "voice": "openai:onyx"},
      {"speaker": "alice", "text": "Hello! I am Alice.", "voice": "openai:nova"}
    ],
    "default_voice": "openai:onyx",
    "speed": 1.0,
    "on_error": "abort",
    "pause_between_speakers": 0.3,
    "output_format": "multi_track"
  }' \
  --output script.json

Response (multi_track, 200):

{
  "tracks": {
    "narrator": "<base64 WAV>",
    "alice": "<base64 WAV>"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "total_duration_s": 4.523,
    "speakers_unique": 2,
    "segment_count": 2,
    "skipped_segments": [],
    "segments": [
      {"index": 0, "speaker": "narrator", "offset_s": 0.0, "duration_s": 1.812},
      {"index": 1, "speaker": "alice", "offset_s": 2.112, "duration_s": 1.411}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Using clone profiles in scripts
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/script \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "script": [
      {"speaker": "host", "text": "Welcome to our podcast.", "voice": "clone:host_voice"},
      {"speaker": "guest", "text": "Thank you for having me.", "voice": "clone:guest_voice"}
    ],
    "default_voice": "clone:host_voice",
    "speed": 1.0,
    "on_error": "skip",
    "pause_between_speakers": 0.5,
    "output_format": "single_track",
    "response_format": "wav"
  }' \
  --output podcast.wav

docs.title: Error handling: skip vs abort
docs.text:
# "skip" — continue on segment failure, list skipped indices
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/script \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "script": [...],
    "on_error": "skip",
    "output_format": "single_track"
  }'

# "abort" — stop on first segment failure (default)

Request Body:

Parameter Type Required Default Range Description script array Yes — 1–100 segments Array of segment objects default_voice string No null Voice ID Default voice for segments without explicitvoice speed float No 1.0 0.25–4.0 Speech speed multiplier (applies to all segments) response_format string No "wav" mp3, opus, aac, flac, wav, pcm Audio format (single_track only) output_format string No "single_track" single_track, multi_track Output mode pause_between_speakers float No 0.5 0.0–5.0 Silence (seconds) inserted on speaker change on_error string No "abort" abort, skip Error handling strategy

Segment Object:

Field Type Required Default Range Description speaker string Yes — 1–64 chars,[a-zA-Z0-9_-] Speaker identifier text string Yes — 1–10,000 chars Text to synthesize voice string No null Voice ID Per-segment voice override speed float No null (inherits) 0.25–4.0 Per-segment speed override

Constraints:

  • Max 100 segments per request
  • Max 50,000 total input characters
  • Max 10 unique speakers
  • Max estimated audio duration: 600 seconds
  • Total timeout: 600 seconds

Response Headers (single_track):

Header Description X-Audio-Duration-S Total mixed audio duration X-Synthesis-Latency-S Total synthesis latency X-Speakers-Unique Number of unique speakers X-Segment-Count Number of synthesized segments X-Skipped-Segments Comma-separated list of skipped segment indices (ifon_error: "skip")

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
OpenAI-compatible preset names mapped to OmniVoice design prompts:

Preset Gender Age Pitch Accent alloy female young adult moderate american ash male young adult low american ballad male middle-aged low british cedar male middle-aged low american coral female young adult high australian echo male middle-aged moderate canadian fable female middle-aged moderate british marin female middle-aged moderate canadian nova female young adult high american onyx male middle-aged very low british sage female elderly low british shimmer female young adult very high american verse male young adult moderate british
